papers.title: Long-term trends and post-pandemic deviations in cervical cancer burden in South India, 1990-2023: a Global Burden of Disease 2023 study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge in India despite advances in prevention through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and screening. Although national estimates indicate gradual declines, marked regional disparities persist, and coronavirus disease 2019-related disruptions may have affected recent disease trajectories. This study assessed long-term trends, post-pandemic deviations, and progress toward World Health Organization (WHO) elimination targets in South India. METHODS: This population-based observational analysis used Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 estimates for women aged 30-69 years in South India from 1990 to 2023. Pre-pandemic trends and counterfactual projections were evaluated, and age-standardized incidence rates (ASRs) were descriptively compared with the WHO elimination threshold of ≤4 cases per 100,000 woman-years. RESULTS: Age-standardized cervical cancer incidence and mortality declined until the early 2010s but remained above national and global rates. Thereafter, declines stagnated and reversed. In 2023, incidence ranged from 26.1 per 100,000 women in Kerala to 65.8 in Telangana; all states exceeded the WHO threshold based on these ASRs. Observed rates exceeded counterfactual projections, but uncertainty envelopes included zero for every location and outcome. Thus, the findings are consistent with possible post-pandemic disruption to cervical cancer services rather than statistically demonstrated excess burden, and this ecological comparison cannot establish causality. Disability-adjusted life-year rates were highest among women aged 50-69 years. CONCLUSION: South India appears to have experienced a recent loss of momentum in cervical cancer control. Strengthening HPV vaccination coverage, expanding screening, and improving the resilience of cancer prevention services are essential for accelerating progress toward elimination targets.
papers.journal: Osong Public Health and Research Perspectives

papers.title_zh: 1990-2023年印度南部宫颈癌负担的长期趋势及疫情后偏离:一项《2023年全球疾病负担》研究
papers.source_body_en: OBJECTIVES: Cervical cancer remains a major public health challenge in India despite advances in prevention through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and screening. Although national estimates indicate gradual declines, marked regional disparities persist, and coronavirus disease 2019-related disruptions may have affected recent disease trajectories. This study assessed long-term trends, post-pandemic deviations, and progress toward World Health Organization (WHO) elimination targets in South India. METHODS: This population-based observational analysis used Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 estimates for women aged 30-69 years in South India from 1990 to 2023. Pre-pandemic trends and counterfactual projections were evaluated, and age-standardized incidence rates (ASRs) were descriptively compared with the WHO elimination threshold of ≤4 cases per 100,000 woman-years. RESULTS: Age-standardized cervical cancer incidence and mortality declined until the early 2010s but remained above national and global rates. Thereafter, declines stagnated and reversed. In 2023, incidence ranged from 26.1 per 100,000 women in Kerala to 65.8 in Telangana; all states exceeded the WHO threshold based on these ASRs. Observed rates exceeded counterfactual projections, but uncertainty envelopes included zero for every location and outcome. Thus, the findings are consistent with possible post-pandemic disruption to cervical cancer services rather than statistically demonstrated excess burden, and this ecological comparison cannot establish causality. Disability-adjusted life-year rates were highest among women aged 50-69 years. CONCLUSION: South India appears to have experienced a recent loss of momentum in cervical cancer control. Strengthening HPV vaccination coverage, expanding screening, and improving the resilience of cancer prevention services are essential for accelerating progress toward elimination targets.
papers.abstract_zh: 目标:尽管通过 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 疫苗接种 和筛查在预防方面取得了进展,但 宫颈癌 仍然是印度的一项重大公共卫生挑战。尽管全国估计数据显示逐渐下降,但显着的地区差异仍然存在,并且与 2019 年冠状病毒病相关的破坏可能影响了近期的疾病轨迹。这项研究评估了印度南部的长期趋势、大流行后的偏差以及世界卫生组织 (WHO) 消除目标的进展情况。方法:这项基于人群的观察分析使用了《2023 年全球疾病负担研究》对 1990 年至 2023 年印度南部 30-69 岁女性的估计。评估了大流行前的趋势和反事实预测,并将年龄标准化的 发病率 率 (ASR) 与世界卫生组织每 100,000 名女性年 ≤ 4 例病例的消除阈值进行了描述性比较。结果:年龄标准化的 宫颈癌、发病率 和 死亡率 直到 2010 年代初才有所下降,但仍高于国家和全球水平。此后,跌势停滞并出现逆转。2023 年,发病率 的范围从喀拉拉邦每 10 万名女性 26.1 人到特伦甘纳邦每 10 万名女性 65.8 人;根据这些 ASR,所有州都超过了 WHO 的阈值。观察到的比率超出了反事实预测,但每个地点和结果的不确定性范围都为零。因此,研究结果与大流行后 宫颈癌 服务可能受到的破坏一致,而不是统计上证明的过度负担,并且这种生态比较无法建立因果关系。50-69 岁女性的残疾调整生命年率最高。结论:南印度最近似乎经历了 宫颈癌 控制势头的丧失。加强 HPV 疫苗接种 覆盖范围、扩大筛查范围和提高癌症预防服务的弹性对于加快实现消除目标至关重要。

papers.title: Immunologic Response and Clinical Course After Off-label Nonavalent HPV Vaccination in Juvenile-onset Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Patients.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JoRRP) is a rare airway disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly HPV6 or HPV11. Affected children often require repeated surgical procedures, and no curative therapy exists. Off-label HPV vaccination has been proposed as an adjunctive treatment, but vaccine-induced immune responses and the relevance of circulating HPV DNA in benign disease remain unclear. METHODS: We longitudinally evaluated 2 children with JoRRP who received off-label nonavalent HPV vaccination between 2020 and 2025. Serum HPV-specific binding and neutralizing antibodies were measured before vaccination and after the second and third doses using multiplex serology and a pseudovirion-based neutralization assay. During bronchoscopic follow-up, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and available biopsy samples were analyzed for HPV DNA. In 1 patient, plasma was additionally tested for circulating HPV DNA by digital polymerase chain reaction. RESULTS: Both children had low or undetectable HPV-specific antibodies at baseline. Vaccination induced strong binding and neutralizing antibody responses against vaccine-included HPV types. During post-vaccination follow-up of 12-29 months after completion of the vaccination series, HPV DNA became undetectable in bronchoalveolar lavage samples, and no new papilloma growth was observed after the last post-vaccination intervention. Circulating HPV DNA was not detected at any time point in the patient tested. CONCLUSIONS: Nonavalent HPV vaccination induced robust neutralizing antibody responses in children with JoRRP and was temporally associated with clinical stabilization. Larger studies are needed to clarify clinical benefit and biomarker utility.

Off-label HPV vaccination has been proposed as an adjunctive treatment, but vaccine-induced immune responses and the relevance of circulating HPV DNA in benign disease remain unclear. Methods We longitudinally evaluated 2 children with JoRRP who received off-label nonavalent HPV vaccination between 2020 and 2025. Serum HPV-specific binding and neutralizing antibodies were measured before vaccination and after the second and third doses using multiplex serology and a pseudovirion-based neutralization assay. During bronchoscopic follow-up, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and available biopsy samples were analyzed for HPV DNA. In 1 patient, plasma was additionally tested for circulating HPV DNA by digital polymerase chain reaction. Results Both children had low or undetectable HPV-specific antibodies at baseline. Vaccination induced strong binding and neutralizing antibody responses against vaccine-included HPV types. During post-vaccination follow-up of 12-29 months after completion of the vaccination series, HPV DNA became undetectable in bronchoalveolar lavage samples, and no new papilloma growth was observed after the last post-vaccination intervention. Circulating HPV DNA was not detected at any time point in the patient tested. Conclusions Nonavalent HPV vaccination induced robust neutralizing antibody responses in children with JoRRP and was temporally associated with clinical stabilization. Larger studies are needed to clarify clinical benefit and biomarker utility.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the immunologic response and clinical course of off-label nonavalent HPV vaccination in two children with juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JoRRP). JoRRP is a rare airway disease caused by HPV, most commonly HPV6 or HPV11, and affected children often require repeated surgical interventions with no curative therapy available. Post-vaccination follow-up showed that HPV DNA became undetectable in bronchoalveolar lavage samples, and no new papilloma growth was observed. Circulating HPV DNA was not detected in one patient. The authors concluded that nonavalent HPV vaccination induced robust neutralizing antibody responses and was temporally associated with clinical stabilization in JoRRP patients. However, they emphasized the need for larger studies to confirm clinical benefit and biomarker utility due to the small sample size and lack of a control group.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:幼年发病复发性呼吸道乳头状瘤病(JoRRP)是一种由人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)引起的罕见气道疾病,最常见的病原体为HPV6或HPV11。受影响的儿童通常需要反复进行手术治疗,且目前尚无治愈性疗法。非标签适应症下的人乳头瘤病毒疫苗已被提出作为辅助治疗手段,但疫苗诱导的免疫应答及循环HPV DNA在良性疾病中的相关性仍不明确。方法:我们对2020年至2025年间接受非标签适应症九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗接种的2名JoRRP患儿进行了纵向评估。在疫苗接种前及接种第二、第三剂后,使用多重血清学检测和假病毒中和试验检测血清中HPV特异性结合抗体与中和抗体。在支气管镜随访期间,对支气管肺泡灌洗液及可用的活检标本进行HPV DNA检测。其中1名患者的血浆样本还通过数字聚合酶链反应检测循环HPV DNA。结果:两名患儿在基线时HPV特异性抗体水平低或检测不到。九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗诱导了针对疫苗所含HPV型别的强效结合抗体与中和抗体应答。在完成疫苗接种后12至29个月的随访期间,支气管肺泡灌洗液样本中HPV DNA变为不可检测,且在最后一次疫苗接种后干预后未观察到新的乳头状瘤生长。在接受检测的患者中,循环HPV DNA在任何时间点均未被检测到。结论:九价人乳头瘤病毒疫苗在JoRRP患儿中诱导了强效中和抗体应答,并与临床稳定存在时间关联。需开展更大规模研究以明确其临床获益及生物标志物应用价值。

papers.title: Oncoviruses at the Crossroads of Ageing and Cancer: Molecular Mechanisms and Key Signalling Pathways.
papers.abstract: Oncoviruses are responsible for a substantial fraction of human cancers and have emerged as critical modulators of host cellular pathways that also govern ageing. The convergence of viral oncogenesis, ageing, and cancer reflects shared molecular mechanisms, including genomic instability, epigenetic alterations, telomere attrition, and chronic inflammation. Increasing evidence indicates that oncoviruses such as human papillomavirus, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B and C viruses, and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus actively reprogramme host signalling networks to promote persistent infection, immune evasion, and malignant transformation. This review synthesises current knowledge on how oncoviruses intersect with key hallmarks of ageing and cancer, with particular emphasis on the signalling pathways that bridge these processes. Central pathways, including p53, mTOR, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT, and Wnt/β-catenin, are frequently targeted by viral proteins, leading to dysregulated cell survival, proliferation, and senescence. These interactions not only facilitate tumourigenesis but also accelerate ageing-associated cellular dysfunctions, such as immunosenescence and inflammaging. Furthermore, we discuss how virus-induced modulation of the tumour microenvironment and host immune responses contributes to the dynamic interplay between ageing and cancer. Understanding these interconnected pathways provides valuable insights into the dual role of oncoviruses as drivers of both age-related decline and cancer development. Elucidating these mechanisms may reveal novel therapeutic targets and strategies for preventing and treating virus-associated malignancies in ageing populations.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 这篇综述探讨了 人乳头瘤病毒 (HPV) 与衰老和癌症关键标志相交叉的分子机制,重点关注桥接这些过程的信号通路。核心问题是 HPV 如何调节 宿主 细胞通路以促进持续感染、免疫逃避和恶性转化,重点是其在与年龄相关的细胞功能障碍中的作用。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是对 HPV 在衰老和癌症中作用的当前知识的叙述性综合。它不报告特定的数据库、搜索日期或荟萃分析方法。这些证据源自对 HPV 及其分子相互作用的现有文献的一般科学理解和解释。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 人们一致认为,包括 HPV 在内的肿瘤病毒会主动重编程 宿主 信号网络,以促进持续感染、免疫逃避和恶性转化。p53、mTOR、NF-κB、PI3K/AKT 和 Wnt/β-连环蛋白等中央通路经常成为病毒蛋白的目标,导致细胞存活、增殖和衰老失调。这些相互作用导致肿瘤发生和衰老相关的细胞功能障碍。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述强调,病毒肿瘤发生、衰老和癌症的趋同反映了共同的分子机制,但证据并未报告具体的争议或相互矛盾的发现。对于病毒诱导的肿瘤微环境调节的精确机制和宿主 免疫应答缺乏详细的讨论。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 了解这些相互关联的途径可能会揭示预防和治疗老龄化人群中与病毒相关的恶性肿瘤的新治疗靶点和策略。该综述表明,需要进一步研究来探索病毒诱导的肿瘤微环境调节与 宿主 免疫应答 之间的动态相互作用。

papers.abstract_zh: 肿瘤病毒是导致大部分人类癌症的原因,并且已成为 宿主 细胞途径的关键调节剂,该途径也控制着衰老。病毒肿瘤发生、衰老和癌症的融合反映了共同的分子机制,包括基因组不稳定性、表观遗传改变、端粒磨损和慢性炎症。越来越多的证据表明,人乳头瘤病毒、Epstein-Barr病毒、乙型和丙型肝炎病毒以及卡波西肉瘤相关疱疹病毒等肿瘤病毒会主动重编程宿主信号网络,以促进持续感染、免疫逃避和恶性转化。这篇综述综合了目前关于肿瘤病毒如何与衰老和癌症的关键特征相交叉的知识,特别强调了桥接这些过程的信号通路。包括 p53、mTOR、NF-κB、PI3K/AKT 和 Wnt/β-catenin 在内的中央通路经常成为病毒蛋白的目标,导致细胞存活、增殖和衰老失调。这些相互作用不仅促进肿瘤发生,而且加速与衰老相关的细胞功能障碍,例如免疫衰老和炎症。此外,我们讨论了病毒诱导的肿瘤微环境调节和 宿主 免疫应答 如何促进衰老与癌症之间的动态相互作用。了解这些相互关联的途径可以为了解肿瘤病毒作为与年龄相关的衰退和癌症发展的驱动因素的双重作用提供有价值的见解。阐明这些机制可能会揭示预防和治疗老龄化人群中与病毒相关的恶性肿瘤的新治疗靶点和策略。

papers.title: HPV vaccine effectiveness against prevalent HPV by age, years sexually active before vaccination, and HIV status in gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, 2019-2021
papers.abstract: Abstract Background We compared the prevalence of vaccine-preventable anal human papillomavirus (HPV) types among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBM) living in large cities in Canada from 2019 to 2021 by age and HIV status. Methods Sexually-active GBM ≥16 years were recruited in Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver using respondent-driven sampling (RDS). Participants self-reported HPV vaccination and self-collected anal HPV specimens. We estimated the prevalence of vaccine-preventable types for participants during the 2019 to 2021 period. elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估HPV疫苗对男男性接触者(GBM)人群中常见HPV感染的预防效果,并按年龄、性活跃年限及HIV状态进行分层分析,这些因素可能影响HPV疫苗的效果。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为一项横断面研究,于2019年至2021年间在加拿大蒙特利尔、多伦多和温哥华通过受试者驱动抽样(RDS)招募≥16岁性活跃GBM参与者。
elements_zh.methods: 参与者自我报告 HPV 疫苗接种 状态并收集自己的肛门 HPV 标本。使用 RDS-II 加权方法估计 患病率,并使用多变量泊松回归计算 患病率 比率 (aPR) 以调整混杂因素。

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究受限于HPV疫苗接种史的自述数据及RDS抽样方法可能引入的偏倚。尽管如此,由于样本量较大且采用统计调整,证据强度为中等。

We report RDS-II-weighted prevalence and confounder-adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) comparing vaccinated (≥1 dose) and unvaccinated GBM using multivariable Poisson regression. Results Among 1,159 participants aged 18-83 (median 35 years), 17.6% were living with HIV, and 62.2%, 40.2% and 15.0% were vaccinated in the 16-26, 27-45, and ≥46-year groups, respectively. Among GBM 16-26 years, HPV6/11/16/18 prevalence was lower among those vaccinated ≤23 years (aPR= 0.40, 95% CI: 0.20-0.77), ≥3 years since first dose (aPR=0.39; 95% CI: 0.18-0.85), and those with ≤5 years of sexual activity before vaccination (aPR=0.47; 95%CI: 0.25-0.89). HPV6/11/16/18/31/33/45/52/58 prevalence was lower among those vaccinated ≤26 years in GBM aged 27-45 years (aPR= 0.81, 95% CI, 0.61-1.08), though this did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions Five years after implementation of Canadian HPV vaccination programs for younger GBM, anal HPV prevalence was lower among those vaccinated at younger ages and near sexual debut.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估HPV疫苗对男男性接触者(GBM)人群中常见HPV感染的预防效果,并按年龄、性活跃年限及HIV状态进行分层分析,这些因素可能影响HPV疫苗的效果。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为一项横断面研究,于2019年至2021年间在加拿大蒙特利尔、多伦多和温哥华通过受试者驱动抽样(RDS)招募≥16岁性活跃GBM参与者。
analysis_zh.methods: 参与者自我报告 HPV 疫苗接种 状态并收集自己的肛门 HPV 标本。使用 RDS-II 加权方法估计 患病率,并使用多变量泊松回归计算 患病率 比率 (aPR) 以调整混杂因素。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在1,159名年龄为18-83岁的参与者中,17.6%为HIV感染者,且HPV疫苗接种率在不同年龄组存在差异:16-26岁、27-45岁及≥46岁年龄组的接种率分别为62.2%、40.2%和15.0%。在16-26岁GBM中,HPV6/11/16/18感染率在≤23岁时接种及性活跃年限≤5年者中显著降低。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,在更年轻年龄及接近性活跃起始时接种HPV疫苗,可降低GBM人群中可通过HPV疫苗预防的HPV感染率,强调了该人群中早期疫苗接种的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 本研究结果为GBM人群的HPV疫苗接种策略提供科学依据,强调了在更年轻个体及性活跃年限较短者中接种疫苗的潜在效益。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究受限于HPV疫苗接种史的自述数据及RDS抽样方法可能引入的偏倚。尽管如此,由于样本量较大且采用统计调整,证据强度为中等。

news.excerpt: Three new studies add to a growing body of research showing that men and boys vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV) are much less likely than others to be infected with the ubiquitous ...
news.rss_summary_html: Three new studies add to a growing body of research showing that men and boys vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV) are much less likely than others to be infected with the ubiquitous ...

news.relevance_llm_reason: record reports HPV vaccines and their benefits for men, which is directly related to HPV infection.
news.content_title: Studies provide more evidence that HPV vaccines benefit men
news.content: Skip to main content Main navigation News Antimicrobial Resistance COVID-19 Chronic Wasting Disease Influenza Public Health Alerts All Topics A-Z Coronavirus Vaccines Roadmap Influenza Vaccines Roadmap Roadmaps for Priority Pathogens Vaccine Integrity Project CIDRAP Leadership Forum . . Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Studies provide more evidence that HPV vaccines benefit men Liz Szabo, MA Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Drs Producoes/iStock Share Copied to clipboard Three new studies add to a growing body of research showing that men and boys vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV) are much less likely than others to be infected with the ubiquitous virus, which can cause cancers of the head and neck, anus, and penis, as well as genital warts. A randomized trial from Japan, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases earlier this month, found that Gardasil 9—which protects against nine HPV strains—dramatically reduced the risk of developing anal or genital HPV infections. The vaccine prevented 92% of persistent infections with the most common strains of HPV and 73% caused by strains that are less common but still able to cause cancer. The researchers followed more than 1,000 men for a median of 2.4 years. A real-world study from Canada, published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases yesterday, focused on gay and bisexual men ages 16 to 23. The study of nearly 1,200 men confirmed that HPV vaccination is most effective when given at a young age, before people are exposed to the virus. Men vaccinated by age 23 were 60% less likely to have anal HPV infections than others in the study. The researchers found no reduction in HPV risk among men vaccinated at age 27 or older. A review of 21 studies performed from 2007 to 2024, published in The International Journal of Infectious Diseases last week, found that HPV vaccinations prevent anal, penile, and oral infections in men. Studies included Gardail 9, as well as an earlier vaccine that prevented four HPV strains. While results varied from study to study, researchers from University of Florida and Merck Research Laboratories found that evidence suggests that vaccines provide good protection, ranging from a 51% reduction in the risk of penile HPV infections to a 100% reduction in the risk of oral HPV infections. Merck is the manufacturer of Gardasil 9. “It’s exciting,” Neil Gross, MD, director of clinical research in the department of head and neck surgery at MD Anderson Cancer Center, told CIDRAP News when asked about the new findings. “We’ve known vaccination is the right thing to do,” said Gross, who was not involved in the studies. “That’s why HPV is recommended as a gender-neutral vaccination strategy. It’s nice to see some data quantifying the benefit.” Good news for men and public health HPV affects about 80% of sexually active women and more than 90% of men. A small number of people develop persistent HPV infections, which can lead to cancer. HPV spreads through intimate contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral sex, and even deep kissing. The randomized, controlled trial from Japan “demonstrates that there is real-world, personal benefit to HPV vaccination for boys and men,” said Demetre Daskalakis, MD, MPH, chief medical officer at the Callen-Lorde Community Health Center in New York, which provides LGBTQ health care. “Vaccination prevented persistent infections which can be associated with cancers... regardless of the gender of sexual partners,” said Daskalakis, former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. The systematic review also “re-affirms the observation that the HPV vaccine is good for public health by interrupting the chain of sexual transmission,” said Daskalakis, who was not involved in the new research. The studies illustrate why it’s important to vaccinate people before they are sexually active, Daskalakis said. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends boys and girls begin the HPV vaccine series at ages 9 to 12 years. “Planning for HPV cancer prevention is like packing an umbrella before the rain starts,” Daskalakis said. “We know that most people will eventually become sexually active, so it's smartest to prepare before the exposure happens.” Evidence to change vaccine policy In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved HPV shots for girls in 2007 and for boys in 2011. About 78% of teens have received one or more doses of the vaccine, although only 63% have received all recommended doses. Children receive two to three doses of the HPV vaccine, depending on the age at which they’re first vaccinated. Planning for HPV cancer prevention is like packing an umbrella before the rain starts. At least 85 countries now offer HPV vaccines to both boys and girls. But there are huge gaps in coverage. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that none of the boys in the Eastern Mediterranean and Southeast Asia have completed the three-dose HPV vaccine regimen, while only 1% of boys have in the African and Pacific regions. Although Japan approved HPV shots for boys in 2020, the vaccines are not yet part of the country’s recommended and subsidized routine vaccination program. Taito Kitano, DrPH, a researcher at Nara Prefecture General Medical Center in Nara, Japan, described the new studies as “important evidence indicating the beneficial impacts of HPV vaccination in males.” Kitano, who also was not involved in the new studies, said, “these data explain why we are recommending HPV vaccination in boys, as well.” In a review published in April, Kitano and his colleagues found that vaccination was linked to a nearly 50% drop in the risk of any HPV-related cancer in men. Because HPV-related tumors can take decades to develop, there are relatively few studies showing changes in cancer or even pre-cancer rates. Given the results of studies like those published this year, many experts predict that future studies will also find that HPV vaccines protect men from anal, penile, and oral cancers. Although research shows that HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer, there is much less evidence about other cancer types. Studying cervical cancer in vaccinated women is easier, because those cancers often develop when women are in their 30s. Head and neck cancers tend to be diagnosed in men in their 60s. “Vaccination programs started in girls and were implemented later in boys,” wrote Miyuki Sawata, PhD, and Alain Luxembourg, MD, PhD, two of the authors of the randomized trial of Gardasil 9 in Japan, in an email. “It is expected that it will take a few more years to observe a decrease in non-cervical cancers related to HPV in vaccinated populations.” A randomized trial in China is expected to help answer these questions by 2029. The study will compare rates of anogenital cancers and precancers in vaccinated and unvaccinated men. Another ongoing international trial, scheduled to conclude in 2028, will measure rates of persistent HPV-related oral infections in men vaccinated with Gardasil 9 and in unvaccinated men. A very common virus Preventing head and neck cancers is particularly important, because there are no proven ways to screen for these tumors, which can develop deep in the throat or on the back of the tongue, Gross said. Many head and neck cancers are found only after becoming advanced, when harsh treatments are necessary. “We don’t have a Pap smear for the throat,” Gross said. People with head and neck cancers experience “a big impact on quality of life and function, and the ability to participate in society the way they did before,” he said. Surveys show that relatively few people have heard of HPV. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Studies provide more evidence that HPV vaccines benefit men Liz Szabo, MA Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Drs Producoes/iStock Share Copied to clipboard Three new studies add to a growing body of research showing that men and boys vaccinated against the human papillomavirus (HPV) are much less likely than others to be infected with the ubiquitous virus, which can cause cancers of the head and neck, anus, and penis, as well as genital warts. A randomized trial from Japan, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases earlier this month, found that Gardasil 9—which protects against nine HPV strains—dramatically reduced the risk of developing anal or genital HPV infections. The vaccine prevented 92% of persistent infections with the most common strains of HPV and 73% caused by strains that are less common but still able to cause cancer. The researchers followed more than 1,000 men for a median of 2.4 years. A real-world study from Canada, published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases yesterday, focused on gay and bisexual men ages 16 to 23. The study of nearly 1,200 men confirmed that HPV vaccination is most effective when given at a young age, before people are exposed to the virus. Men vaccinated by age 23 were 60% less likely to have anal HPV infections than others in the study. The researchers found no reduction in HPV risk among men vaccinated at age 27 or older. A review of 21 studies performed from 2007 to 2024, published in The International Journal of Infectious Diseases last week, found that HPV vaccinations prevent anal, penile, and oral infections in men. Studies included Gardail 9, as well as an earlier vaccine that prevented four HPV strains. While results varied from study to study, researchers from University of Florida and Merck Research Laboratories found that evidence suggests that vaccines provide good protection, ranging from a 51% reduction in the risk of penile HPV infections to a 100% reduction in the risk of oral HPV infections. Merck is the manufacturer of Gardasil 9. “It’s exciting,” Neil Gross, MD, director of clinical research in the department of head and neck surgery at MD Anderson Cancer Center, told CIDRAP News when asked about the new findings. “We’ve known vaccination is the right thing to do,” said Gross, who was not involved in the studies. “That’s why HPV is recommended as a gender-neutral vaccination strategy. It’s nice to see some data quantifying the benefit.” Good news for men and public health HPV affects about 80% of sexually active women and more than 90% of men. A small number of people develop persistent HPV infections, which can lead to cancer. HPV spreads through intimate contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral sex, and even deep kissing. The randomized, controlled trial from Japan “demonstrates that there is real-world, personal benefit to HPV vaccination for boys and men,” said Demetre Daskalakis, MD, MPH, chief medical officer at the Callen-Lorde Community Health Center in New York, which provides LGBTQ health care. “Vaccination prevented persistent infections which can be associated with cancers... regardless of the gender of sexual partners,” said Daskalakis, former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. The systematic review also “re-affirms the observation that the HPV vaccine is good for public health by interrupting the chain of sexual transmission,” said Daskalakis, who was not involved in the new research. The studies illustrate why it’s important to vaccinate people before they are sexually active, Daskalakis said. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends boys and girls begin the HPV vaccine series at ages 9 to 12 years. “Planning for HPV cancer prevention is like packing an umbrella before the rain starts,” Daskalakis said. “We know that most people will eventually become sexually active, so it's smartest to prepare before the exposure happens.” Evidence to change vaccine policy In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved HPV shots for girls in 2007 and for boys in 2011. About 78% of teens have received one or more doses of the vaccine, although only 63% have received all recommended doses. Children receive two to three doses of the HPV vaccine, depending on the age at which they’re first vaccinated. Planning for HPV cancer prevention is like packing an umbrella before the rain starts. At least 85 countries now offer HPV vaccines to both boys and girls. But there are huge gaps in coverage. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that none of the boys in the Eastern Mediterranean and Southeast Asia have completed the three-dose HPV vaccine regimen, while only 1% of boys have in the African and Pacific regions. Although Japan approved HPV shots for boys in 2020, the vaccines are not yet part of the country’s recommended and subsidized routine vaccination program. Because HPV-related tumors can take decades to develop, there are relatively few studies showing changes in cancer or even pre-cancer rates. Given the results of studies like those published this year, many experts predict that future studies will also find that HPV vaccines protect men from anal, penile, and oral cancers. Although research shows that HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer, there is much less evidence about other cancer types. Studying cervical cancer in vaccinated women is easier, because those cancers often develop when women are in their 30s. The study will compare rates of anogenital cancers and precancers in vaccinated and unvaccinated men. Another ongoing international trial, scheduled to conclude in 2028, will measure rates of persistent HPV-related oral infections in men vaccinated with Gardasil 9 and in unvaccinated men. Many head and neck cancers are found only after becoming advanced, when harsh treatments are necessary. “We don’t have a Pap smear for the throat,” Gross said. analysis.time: The studies were published in 2026, with the Japanese trial published earlier this month and the Canadian study published yesterday. The randomized trial was followed for a median of 2.4 years.
analysis.location_and_population: The studies involved men in Japan and Canada, with the Japanese trial focusing on men aged 16 to 26 and the Canadian study on gay and bisexual men aged 16 to 23. The systematic review included 21 studies from 2007 to 2024.
analysis.event: Three new studies show that HPV vaccines significantly reduce the risk of anal and genital HPV infections in men. A randomized trial from Japan found Gardasil 9 reduced the risk of developing anal or genital HPV infections, and a real-world study from Canada confirmed the effectiveness of vaccination in younger men.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The vaccine prevented 92% of persistent infections with the most common HPV strains and 73% of infections caused by less common but cancer-associated strains. It also showed a 51% to 100% reduction in the risk of penile and oral HPV infections, respectively.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The studies are ongoing, with the Japanese trial following participants for 2.4 years. The researchers noted that future studies will likely confirm the protective effects against HPV-related cancers. The WHO estimates coverage gaps in boys, particularly in certain regions.

analysis.brief_en: Recent studies provide more evidence that HPV vaccines benefit men by significantly reducing the risk of anal and genital HPV infections. A Japanese randomized trial found Gardasil 9 prevented 92% of persistent infections with common HPV strains and 73% of those linked to cancer. A Canadian real-world study confirmed that men vaccinated by age 23 had a 60% lower risk of anal HPV infections, while those vaccinated later showed no reduction. The vaccine also demonstrated a 51% to 100% risk reduction for penile and oral infections, respectively. These findings support the recommendation for gender-neutral HPV vaccination strategies, as early vaccination is most effective. However, coverage gaps persist globally, with limited access in regions like the Eastern Mediterranean and Southeast Asia. The studies highlight the importance of vaccinating before sexual activity begins, as HPV-related cancers can develop over decades. Future research, including a Chinese trial expected by 2029, may further confirm these protective effects against cancers such as anal, penile, and oral cancers.

news.content_zh: 近期研究为人乳头瘤病毒疫苗(HPV疫苗)对男性的益处提供了更多证据,显示其可显著降低肛门和生殖器HPV感染风险。一项日本随机试验发现,九价HPV疫苗(Gardasil 9)可预防92%的常见HPV持续性感染,以及73%的与癌症相关HPV感染。加拿大一项真实世界研究证实,23岁前接种疫苗的男性罹患肛门HPV感染的风险降低60%,而晚期接种者则无降低效果。HPV疫苗还可将阴茎和口腔感染风险分别降低51%至100%。这些发现支持采用HPV疫苗性别中和策略的建议,因早期接种效果最佳。然而,全球覆盖率仍存在缺口,东地中海和东南亚等地区接种受限。研究强调应在性活动开始前接种疫苗,因HPV相关癌症可能在数十年后发展。未来研究,包括预计于2029年启动的一项中国试验,可能进一步确认疫苗对肛门癌、阴茎癌和口腔癌等癌症的保护效果。

The approach combines HPV genotyping with measurements of non-coding RNAs—molecules that do not produce proteins but can exert powerful control over gene activity. By reading both the virus and the host cell, researchers argue, screening could move beyond the simple question of whether high-risk HPV is present and begin to estimate whether an infection is biologically active, persistent and potentially dangerous. The distinction matters because infection with a high-risk HPV type is common, while cervical cancer is relatively uncommon among infected individuals. Most HPV infections are transient and are cleared by the immune system without causing lasting cellular damage. A smaller proportion persist, and persistent infection can create the conditions for precancerous lesions and, eventually, invasive cancer. Current screening methods—including HPV DNA testing, cytology and visual examination—have improved early detection, but they do not always identify which positive results represent a short-lived infection and which signal a transformation process already underway. This uncertainty can lead to repeated testing, unnecessary procedures or delayed attention to genuinely high-risk disease. HPV genotyping supplies an important part of the missing information. Rather than reporting only that HPV is present, genotyping identifies the specific viral type or group. Some strains, particularly HPV16 and HPV18, are strongly associated with cervical cancer, while other high-risk types carry different levels of risk. Genotyping is therefore useful for surveillance, triage and evaluating vaccination programs. Yet the viral type alone cannot reveal whether the virus is actively altering the host cell. Two people infected with the same high-risk strain may have very different outcomes, depending on viral persistence, immune responses, viral gene expression and changes accumulating in cervical cells. Discover more cancer Cancer Screening Information Biotechnology News Feed Bioengineering Career Resources Bioengineering News Subscription The proposed second layer of testing focuses on non-coding RNAs, or ncRNAs. These include microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs and circular RNAs, each with distinct molecular properties and functions. MicroRNAs are short RNA molecules that bind to messenger RNAs and usually reduce the production of specific proteins. Long non-coding RNAs can influence gene transcription, organize protein complexes or alter the stability and availability of other RNAs. Circular RNAs form closed loops that can be unusually resistant to degradation and may regulate gene expression by binding microRNAs or interacting with proteins. Together, these molecules create a regulatory network that can reflect how a cervical cell is responding to HPV. The biological connection between HPV and ncRNAs is central to the review’s argument. High-risk HPV produces oncoproteins, particularly E6 and E7, that interfere with cellular safeguards governing genome stability, cell division and programmed cell death. E6 can promote the degradation or functional suppression of the tumor-suppressor protein p53, while E7 disrupts the retinoblastoma pathway, which normally restrains inappropriate entry into the cell cycle. These disturbances can reshape the cell’s transcriptional and post-transcriptional programs. In turn, altered ncRNAs may help sustain proliferation, weaken apoptosis, modify immune signaling and promote invasion—features associated with malignant progression. Several candidate molecules illustrate how such signals might be used. The review discusses microRNAs whose abundance changes in HPV-associated cervical disease, including miR-21, miR-155, miR-375, miR-145 and miR-106b-5p. Some have been linked with enhanced growth, migration or poor prognosis, while others appear to restrain invasion or proliferation and become reduced during disease progression. The molecular effects are not interchangeable: miR-21, for example, has been associated with pathways affecting growth and migration, whereas reduced miR-375 has been linked to loss of control over transcription factor SP1. These patterns could form part of a multi-marker signature rather than serve as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Long non-coding and circular RNAs may add information about the architecture and persistence of the cancer-associated regulatory network. HOTAIR has been associated with cervical cancer progression and has been studied in serum and vaginal discharge, while MALAT1 can be regulated by the HPV16 E7 protein and has been connected to cancer progression, metastasis, immunity and treatment resistance. Other studies summarized in the review describe HPV-related changes in lnc-FANCI-2 and circular RNAs involved in regulatory axes such as miR-1236-3p/TRIM37 and miR-1179/ABL2. Because circular RNAs are structurally stable and many ncRNAs can circulate in blood or other biological fluids, they are attractive candidates for liquid biopsy tests that might avoid or complement tissue sampling. Discover more Colleges & Universities Printing & Publishing Scientific Bioengineering Video Library Science In practice, an integrated test could combine several forms of evidence from one sample. HPV DNA analysis would identify the viral genotype, while RNA profiling could measure a panel of host-response molecules and perhaps indicators of active oncogenic signaling. A computational model could then classify a patient’s result into a lower- or higher-risk category, guiding the interval for repeat screening or the need for colposcopy and biopsy. The same principle could potentially be adapted to self-collected vaginal samples, cervical specimens or blood-based assays, although the review does not present a clinically validated test or a new patient cohort. It describes a diagnostic framework whose usefulness depends on selecting robust markers, standardizing laboratory methods and proving that the combined signal predicts outcomes better than existing screening. That evidence gap is the most important qualification. The authors emphasize that individual ncRNAs have shown promising associations with HPV-mediated carcinogenesis, but evidence for their combined clinical use with HPV genotyping remains limited. Biomarker levels can vary with age, inflammation, hormonal status, sampling technique, disease stage and the composition of the surrounding tissue. Results generated in cell lines or small retrospective studies may not translate directly to diverse populations or routine clinics. Prospective studies will need to follow HPV-positive individuals over time, compare transient and persistent infections, test different viral genotypes and establish thresholds that are reproducible across laboratories. The review also notes that no datasets were generated or analyzed for the study itself, because it is a narrative synthesis of existing evidence. If validated, the strategy could make cervical screening more precise without replacing established prevention tools. HPV vaccination remains fundamental, and conventional HPV testing and cytology remain valuable for identifying people who need further assessment. The promise of ncRNA profiling is to add biological context: not only which virus is present, but how strongly it is influencing the host cell. Such information could reduce the burden of unnecessary follow-up while directing clinical attention toward infections with molecular signs of transformation. For now, the concept is best viewed as an emerging precision-screening platform rather than a ready-to-use diagnostic. Its viral-news appeal lies in a simple idea with complex biology: the future of cervical cancer detection may depend on listening simultaneously to the genome of the virus and the regulatory RNA language of the cell it infects. analysis.time: Published on August 28, 2026; the review was released on that date (evidence N1).
analysis.location_and_population: The article addresses humans infected with high‐risk human papillomavirus, especially women undergoing cervical cancer screening; no specific geographic location is reported (evidence N2, N3, N4).
analysis.event: A review in Molecular Biology Reports proposes combining HPV genotyping with non‐coding RNA profiling to distinguish transient from potentially oncogenic infections. The proposal is presented as a research concept, not a validated clinical test, and the authors note significant evidence gaps (evidence N1, N3, N40, N43).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Most HPV infections are transient and cleared without harm, while a smaller proportion persist and can create conditions for precancerous lesions and invasive cervical cancer. High‐risk HPV infection is common, but cervical cancer remains relatively uncommon among infected individuals (evidence N4, N5, N6).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The strategy remains unvalidated; the review highlights the need for prospective studies to establish thresholds, reproducibility, and clinical utility. Current status is exploratory, with uncertainty about translation to routine practice (evidence N40, N43, N44).

analysis.brief_en: A recent review in Molecular Biology Reports outlines a novel screening concept that merges HPV genotype data with host non‐coding RNA signatures to better predict which infections may progress toward cervical cancer. While HPV genotyping identifies the viral type, non‐coding RNAs such as microRNAs, long non‐coding RNAs, and circular RNAs could reveal whether the virus is actively altering cellular pathways. The authors argue this dual approach could separate transient, low‐risk infections from persistent, high‐risk cases, potentially reducing unnecessary follow‐ups. However, they stress that the method has not yet been clinically validated; existing evidence comes mainly from cell‐line work and small retrospective studies. Prospective, large‐scale trials are needed to confirm its diagnostic value and establish standardized thresholds before routine implementation.

The authors argue this dual approach could separate transient, low‐risk infections from persistent, high‐risk cases, potentially reducing unnecessary follow‐ups. However, they stress that the method has not yet been clinically validated; existing evidence comes mainly from cell‐line work and small retrospective studies. news.title_zh: 结合非编码RNA谱系与HPV基因分型提升宫颈癌风险评估 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A recent review in Molecular Biology Reports outlines a novel screening concept that merges HPV genotype data with host non‐coding RNA signatures to better predict which infections may progress toward cervical cancer. While HPV genotyping identifies the viral type, non‐coding RNAs such as microRNAs, long non‐coding RNAs, and circular RNAs could reveal whether the virus is actively altering cellular pathways. The authors argue this dual approach could separate transient, low‐risk infections from persistent, high‐risk cases, potentially reducing unnecessary follow‐ups. However, they stress that the method has not yet been clinically validated; existing evidence comes mainly from cell‐line work and small retrospective studies. Prospective, large‐scale trials are needed to confirm its diagnostic value and establish standardized thresholds before routine implementation.
news.content_zh: 《分子生物学报告》近期的一篇综述提出了一种新颖的筛查理念,将高危型HPV基因分型数据与宿主非编码RNA特征谱系相结合,以更好地预测哪些感染可能进展为宫颈癌。HPV基因分型可识别病毒类型,而微小RNA、长链非编码RNA及环状RNA等非编码RNA则可揭示病毒是否正在主动改变细胞通路。作者认为,这种双重策略有望将一过性低风险感染与持续性高风险病例区分开来,从而可能减少不必要的随访。然而,他们强调该方法尚未获得临床验证;现有证据主要来自细胞系研究和小规模回顾性研究。需要前瞻性大规模临床试验来确认其诊断价值并建立标准化阈值,方可考虑常规应用。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, August 29, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Study examines HPV antibody durability and immune response after stem cell transplantation by Bioengineer August 27, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A small pilot study from Thailand suggests that adolescents who undergo hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may develop a strong and persistent antibody response after receiving two doses of the human papillomavirus vaccine, challenging the assumption that three doses are always necessary for this medically vulnerable group. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, offer early evidence that a two-dose schedule can produce detectable antibodies against HPV types 16 and 18 in most young transplant recipients, while also maintaining measurable protection for years after vaccination. The results could eventually help doctors refine vaccination schedules for children and teenagers whose immune systems have been rebuilt after intensive cancer or blood-disorder treatment. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or HSCT, is used to replace diseased or damaged blood-forming cells with healthy stem cells. Before the transplant, patients typically receive chemotherapy, total-body irradiation, or both to destroy malignant cells and suppress the immune system so that the donated cells can take hold. This conditioning process also eliminates many of the immune cells and antibody-producing memory cells generated by previous infections or vaccinations. As a result, transplant recipients are often treated as though they have lost much of their earlier vaccine protection and must be revaccinated according to specialized schedules. That issue is particularly important for HPV, a group of viruses transmitted mainly through sexual contact and responsible for nearly all cases of cervical cancer as well as a substantial proportion of anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV vaccines work best when administered before exposure to the virus, which is why routine vaccination focuses on adolescents. In healthy young people, the World Health Organization now recommends a single dose in many settings. Immunocompromised individuals, however, are generally advised to receive three doses because their immune systems may produce a weaker or less durable response. Whether adolescents recovering from HSCT truly need that full three-dose schedule has remained uncertain. Discover more Health Conditions Biological Sciences Health Foundations & Medical Research Cancer Infectious Diseases The research team at Ramathibodi Hospital and Mahidol University in Bangkok investigated the question through two complementary cohorts. The first included 23 adolescents between 9 and 15 years old who were at least one year beyond transplantation and had stopped taking immunosuppressive medicines for at least six months. Each participant received a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, which targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18, at the start of the study and again six months later. Blood samples were collected six months after the first dose and one month after the second dose to determine whether the participants had developed antibodies against HPV16 and HPV18, two high-risk types strongly associated with cancer. The scientists measured antibodies directed against the L1 capsid proteins of HPV16 and HPV18. L1 is the major structural protein forming the outer shell of the virus, and vaccine particles made from virus-like assemblies of L1 train the immune system to recognize the pathogen without containing viral genetic material. The investigators used an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, or ELISA, to detect immunoglobulin G antibodies in blood serum. In practical terms, seroconversion meant that a participant’s antibody index crossed the study’s predefined threshold for a positive result, indicating that vaccination had generated a measurable immune response. Six months after the first dose, the response was incomplete but substantial: 54.5 percent of participants had seroconverted against HPV16, while 68.2 percent had seroconverted against HPV18. The second injection produced a striking increase. One month after the booster, 95.5 percent of adolescents had detectable antibodies against HPV16 and 90.9 percent had detectable antibodies against HPV18. The pattern suggests that the first dose primed the immune system in many participants, while the second dose activated immunological memory and generated a much broader antibody response. This boost is biologically important because antibodies can bind viral particles before they infect epithelial cells, blocking the earliest step in HPV transmission. The vaccination was also well tolerated. Local reactions, such as pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site, were reported by between 22 and 39 percent of participants during the first 48 hours. Systemic reactions were uncommon, and the researchers observed no serious adverse events. For transplant recipients, who may face complications including graft-versus-host disease, recurrent disease, and infections, the absence of serious vaccine-related problems is reassuring. Nevertheless, the safety findings must be interpreted cautiously because the cohort contained only 23 participants and was not large enough to detect rare complications. The study’s second cohort examined whether antibodies remained detectable over time. Fifteen vaccinated adolescents were assessed at intervals ranging from six months to 62 months after their final HPV vaccine dose. Every participant had detectable antibodies against HPV16, and all but one had detectable antibodies against HPV18. The cross-sectional design means that the researchers did not repeatedly follow the same individuals from vaccination onward, so the data cannot establish precisely how antibody concentrations changed in each participant. Even so, the results provide an encouraging snapshot of immune durability extending for more than five years in some adolescents. The authors emphasize that the findings do not yet justify replacing existing recommendations for all HSCT recipients. The study was a pilot investigation with small numbers, no unvaccinated comparison group, and antibody measurements focused on only two HPV types. Detectable antibodies are an important marker of protection, but the relationship between a laboratory antibody index and real-world prevention of HPV infection is not perfectly defined. The participants were also vaccinated after recovering sufficiently from transplantation, and the results may not apply to patients who remain on immunosuppressive therapy or who experience severe immune complications. Larger studies should track antibody titers serially, assess responses to all vaccine-covered HPV types, and compare two-dose and three-dose schedules directly. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, offer early evidence that a two-dose schedule can produce detectable antibodies against HPV types 16 and 18 in most young transplant recipients, while also maintaining measurable protection for years after vaccination. The results could eventually help doctors refine vaccination schedules for children and teenagers whose immune systems have been rebuilt after intensive cancer or blood-disorder treatment. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or HSCT, is used to replace diseased or damaged blood-forming cells with healthy stem cells. Before the transplant, patients typically receive chemotherapy, total-body irradiation, or both to destroy malignant cells and suppress the immune system so that the donated cells can take hold. This conditioning process also eliminates many of the immune cells and antibody-producing memory cells generated by previous infections or vaccinations. As a result, transplant recipients are often treated as though they have lost much of their earlier vaccine protection and must be revaccinated according to specialized schedules. That issue is particularly important for HPV, a group of viruses transmitted mainly through sexual contact and responsible for nearly all cases of cervical cancer as well as a substantial proportion of anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV vaccines work best when administered before exposure to the virus, which is why routine vaccination focuses on adolescents. In healthy young people, the World Health Organization now recommends a single dose in many settings. Immunocompromised individuals, however, are generally advised to receive three doses because their immune systems may produce a weaker or less durable response. Whether adolescents recovering from HSCT truly need that full three-dose schedule has remained uncertain. Discover more Health Conditions Biological Sciences Health Foundations & Medical Research Cancer Infectious Diseases The research team at Ramathibodi Hospital and Mahidol University in Bangkok investigated the question through two complementary cohorts. The first included 23 adolescents between 9 and 15 years old who were at least one year beyond transplantation and had stopped taking immunosuppressive medicines for at least six months. Each participant received a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, which targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18, at the start of the study and again six months later. Blood samples were collected six months after the first dose and one month after the second dose to determine whether the participants had developed antibodies against HPV16 and HPV18, two high-risk types strongly associated with cancer. The scientists measured antibodies directed against the L1 capsid proteins of HPV16 and HPV18. L1 is the major structural protein forming the outer shell of the virus, and vaccine particles made from virus-like assemblies of L1 train the immune system to recognize the pathogen without containing viral genetic material. The investigators used an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, or ELISA, to detect immunoglobulin G antibodies in blood serum. In practical terms, seroconversion meant that a participant’s antibody index crossed the study’s predefined threshold for a positive result, indicating that vaccination had generated a measurable immune response. Six months after the first dose, the response was incomplete but substantial: 54.5 percent of participants had seroconverted against HPV16, while 68.2 percent had seroconverted against HPV18. The second injection produced a striking increase. One month after the booster, 95.5 percent of adolescents had detectable antibodies against HPV16 and 90.9 percent had detectable antibodies against HPV18. The pattern suggests that the first dose primed the immune system in many participants, while the second dose activated immunological memory and generated a much broader antibody response. This boost is biologically important because antibodies can bind viral particles before they infect epithelial cells, blocking the earliest step in HPV transmission. The vaccination was also well tolerated. Local reactions, such as pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site, were reported by between 22 and 39 percent of participants during the first 48 hours. Systemic reactions were uncommon, and the researchers observed no serious adverse events. For transplant recipients, who may face complications including graft-versus-host disease, recurrent disease, and infections, the absence of serious vaccine-related problems is reassuring. Nevertheless, the safety findings must be interpreted cautiously because the cohort contained only 23 participants and was not large enough to detect rare complications. The study’s second cohort examined whether antibodies remained detectable over time. Fifteen vaccinated adolescents were assessed at intervals ranging from six months to 62 months after their final HPV vaccine dose. Every participant had detectable antibodies against HPV16, and all but one had detectable antibodies against HPV18. The cross-sectional design means that the researchers did not repeatedly follow the same individuals from vaccination onward, so the data cannot establish precisely how antibody concentrations changed in each participant. Even so, the results provide an encouraging snapshot of immune durability extending for more than five years in some adolescents. The authors emphasize that the findings do not yet justify replacing existing recommendations for all HSCT recipients. The study was a pilot investigation with small numbers, no unvaccinated comparison group, and antibody measurements focused on only two HPV types. Detectable antibodies are an important marker of protection, but the relationship between a laboratory antibody index and real-world prevention of HPV infection is not perfectly defined. The participants were also vaccinated after recovering sufficiently from transplantation, and the results may not apply to patients who remain on immunosuppressive therapy or who experience severe immune complications. Larger studies should track antibody titers serially, assess responses to all vaccine-covered HPV types, and compare two-dose and three-dose schedules directly. Despite those limitations, the study addresses a growing clinical challenge: how to restore vaccine protection efficiently without subjecting transplant survivors to unnecessary injections. Its results indicate that a two-dose quadrivalent schedule may be capable of producing near-universal antibody responses against HPV16 and HPV18 in selected adolescents once immune recovery has occurred. The evidence is not a final answer, but it supplies a valuable clue for future trials and could help guide individualized vaccination strategies. For young people who have already endured intensive treatment to rebuild their blood and immune systems, preserving protection against a preventable family of cancer-causing viruses may become an increasingly important part of long-term survivorship care. Common myths about the virus linked to cervical cancer Scientists have identified more than 200 types of human papillomavirus, some of which have known links to cancer Copy link Bookmark Comments Go to comments Bookmark popover Removed from bookmarks Close popover Close Powered By 10 Sec 2.6K 00 No cervical cancer cases in young women fully vaccinated with HPV in Scotland Next video in Share Next KEEP WATCHING No cervical cancer cases in young women fully vaccinated with HPV in Scotland This article was originally published by The Conversation in June 2025, and is being republished by the Independent after it was announced that women in England will receive home cervical screening kits for HPV. Few viruses are as widespread – and sometimes misunderstood – as the human papillomavirus, or HPV. It’s so common that most of us – up to 80% – will encounter it at some point in our lives, often without even realising it. Understanding HPV matters, given that it is linked to several types of cancer. Scientists have identified more than 200 types of HPV, making it one of the most diverse viral families known – and a complex one at that. Many strains are low risk, causing either no symptoms or benign warts. HPV types 1, 2 and 4, for instance, are responsible for the common skin wart. Many will have experienced these, including the familiar verruca (plantar wart) picked up at swimming pools. Some strains, such as HPV 6 and 11, cause genital warts – small growths that appear on the genitals or around the anus. Treatments such as creams, surgical removal or freezing can get rid of the visible warts, but they don’t remove the virus itself. This means the virus can still be passed to sexual partners until the body’s immune system clears it. open image in gallery HPV is a DNA virus from the papillomavirus family (Alamy/PA) Most seriously, certain types of HPV – particularly 16 and 18 – have known links to cancer. They belong to a group of about 14 high-risk strains that can enter human cells and damage their DNA. This damage interferes with the cells’ normal controls on growth and division, which can lead to the development of cancer. RECOMMENDED Canada’s Carney responds to Trump’s Lake America name change with a history lesson Dolly Parton’s sister shares insight into country icon’s final months Ask a Pro: "How Long Does $2.5 Million Last in Retirement?"SmartAsset | SponsoredSponsored You'll Never Guess What Melts Tartar Off From Your Dog's Teeth (Not a Toothbrush)Petsnewsdaily | SponsoredSponsored Repeated or persistent infection with these strains increases the risk of developing cancer. So, too, does smoking, which reduces the ability of the immune system to clear the virus. Because HPV comes in so many forms – from harmless skin warts to strains linked with cancer – it’s easy to see how myths and confusion can take hold. To separate fact from fiction, here are five key points that everyone should know about the virus. 1. HPV is not just associated with cervical cancer While cervical cancer remains the most recognised HPV-related malignancy, the virus is also linked to cancers of the vulva, vagina, anus, penis, mouth and throat. Emerging evidence suggests some types may also contribute to developing skin cancer. This broad cancer risk explains why the widely available HPV vaccine is recommended for both sexes. The vaccine’s ability to prevent HPV infection makes population-wide immunisation beneficial, as transmission may occur between heterosexual and homosexual partners alike. 2. You don’t need to have symptoms or genital warts to pass the virus on HPV can remain on the skin for months before the immune system clears it, allowing transmission through contact even before genital warts appear and after they’ve been treated. This is why condoms should be used for at least three months after visible warts have resolved. 3. HPV transmission can occur from more than just vaginal or anal sex Oral and throat cancers can develop following HPV infection acquired through oral sex. The incidence of mouth and throat cancer is increasing worldwide, with oral sex now the most significant behavioural risk factor. Using condoms during oral sex can help reduce this risk. About the author Dan Baumgardt is a Senior Lecturer in the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Bristol. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. HPV can also spread through the use of sex toys. One study highlighted the ability of transmissible HPV to remain on sex toys and the need to develop proper hygiene practices for cleaning, and avoiding shared use. 4. Condoms are not 100% effective at preventing spread Condoms can lower the risk of HPV transmission, but they can’t offer full protection, as uncovered skin can still carry the virus. This is why many sexually active people will come into contact with a strain of the virus at some point in their lives, even when practising safe sex. 5. Even vaccinated women need to have smear tests Current HPV vaccines target the main high-risk virus types but cannot cover all cancer-causing strains, or treat existing infections. In rarer cases, cervical cancer can also arise without HPV infection. This is why women aged 25 to 64 are still invited for cervical screening every five years, even after vaccination. Women should also seek urgent medical review for other indicators of cervical cancer. These include pain or bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods or after menopause, and changes in vaginal discharge. open image in gallery A nurse injects a dose of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine (AFP/Getty) Even though the HPV vaccine is widely available, uptake has dropped in some areas. The COVID pandemic disrupted routine vaccination programmes, while misinformation about the vaccine’s safety and effectiveness has shaken trust. In some places, low awareness of HPV’s link to different cancers – and of the need to vaccinate boys as well as girls – has also made public understanding more difficult. RECOMMENDED Emmerdale viewers left furious after fan favourite character dies Son of former Chelsea star dies hiking in 40C heat Cesar Millan Reveals What Honey Does to Your Aging DogPets Daily Health | SponsoredSponsored One Kitchen Ingredient Removes Tartar From Your Dog's Gum LinePetsnewsdaily | SponsoredSponsored The World Health Organisation has set a target of fully vaccinating 90% of girls by age 15 by 2030. At present, only about 48% of girls worldwide are fully vaccinated, so there is more work to be done. Although HPV is often harmless, the potential consequences of some strains are too significant to ignore. But no one should be fearful of an active sex life. For those eligible for the HPV vaccine, protection is not just for the individual, but also for future sexual partners who could otherwise be exposed. By staying informed and taking preventative measures, we can reduce the effects of this common virus and keep ourselves and others safer. news.title_zh: HPV是什么?与宫颈癌相关的病毒的常见误区 - 《独立报》
news.source_body_en: This article from The Independent provides an overview of human papillomavirus (HPV), emphasizing its widespread nature and its association with various cancers, including cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers. It highlights that HPV is one of the most diverse viral families, with over 200 types identified, some of which are low risk and cause benign warts, while others, such as HPV 16 and 18, are high risk and linked to cancer. The article notes that the HPV vaccine is recommended for both sexes to prevent infection, but it does not cover all cancer-causing strains or treat existing infections. It also mentions that only about 48% of girls worldwide are fully vaccinated, and public health efforts are ongoing to improve vaccination rates. The piece underscores the importance of condoms, hygiene practices, and regular cervical screening, even for vaccinated individuals, to mitigate the risk of HPV transmission and related cancers.
news.content_zh: 本文来自《独立报》,概述了人乳头瘤病毒(人乳头瘤病毒,HPV),强调其广泛传播特性及其与多种癌症(包括宫颈癌、肛门癌和口咽癌)的关联。文中指出,HPV是最多样化的病毒科之一,已确认超过200种型别,其中部分为低风险型,可引发良性疣,而其他型别(如HPV 16型和18型)则为高风险型,与癌症相关。文章提到,HPV疫苗接种建议适用于两性,以预防感染,但疫苗无法覆盖所有致癌株,也不能治疗现有感染。文中还指出,全球仅约48%的女孩完成HPV疫苗全程接种,公共卫生工作正持续推进疫苗接种率。该文强调,即使接种疫苗,仍需采用安全套、良好卫生习惯及定期宫颈癌筛查等措施,以减轻HPV传播及相关癌症的风险。

Millions of women will be sent at-home cervical cancer screening kits for free on the NHS, it was announced today. ‌ Campaigners welcomed the move which will see tests mailed out to those who have not attended screening appointments. Swabs used to collect a sample from the vagina will then posted back to NHS labs for free, where it will be tested for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). ‌ HPV is a group of viruses which can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. However, around 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers. ‌ READ MORE: BBC Race Across The World star dies a year after her son and co-star Sam died in car crash READ MORE: 'I thought I had food poisoning from Egypt holiday but I was seriously ill' View 2 Images The tests will help identify high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) which can cause 99.7% of cervical cancers(Image: Getty Images) Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health at NHS England, said: "Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS. "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game changer - making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV." ‌ Gem Sofianos-Boorman was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28 after taking up her cervical screening invite. She said "it was the last thing" she expected, as she was "young, healthy, and had no symptoms". Ms Sofianos-Boorman, now 39, said: "Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread. "That's why it's great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening. Cervical cancer often doesn't cause symptoms in its early stages, so screening plays a really important role in finding something before it might become serious." ‌ View 2 Images Dr Sue Mann said "screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier" Eligible women aged between 30 and 65, who have not attended screening appointments, will be sent invitations from today through the NHS app, text message, email or by letter. They will then be able to order a kit through the NHS app or online. The phased rollout forms part of the NHS's target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040. Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years depending on their age, or more often if HPV is detected. Latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. ‌ The health service estimates this means around four million women are not up to date. Dr Mann said: "There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening - embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort - and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test. "So, if you're invited to take part, please order a test - it's a simple swab you can do at home in minutes." Athena Lamnisos, chief executive at The Eve Appeal, said: "Cervical screening is designed to prevent cervical cancer rather than respond to symptoms, attending a clinic requires people to actively prioritise an appointment among the many competing demands of everyday life. ‌ "Self-testing which can be done at home will be a step-change for many. We have the incredible opportunity to see the back of cervical cancer. How brilliant would that be? But to achieve this, we need to support everyone eligible to attend screening. "This is not a replacement for clinician screening, and we will continue to work with and support those attending their traditional cervical screening, to help make their appointments more comfortable and accessible." Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Cervical cancer is preventable - but that's why we want to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. These free self-testing kits will be offered to four million women who are currently behind on their screening to make it easier for as many women as possible to keep themselves healthy and safe. Article continues below "This is the future NHS we are building - there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths." Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: "At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them. If people receive their cervical screening or self-testing kit invitation, please consider taking up the offer and encourage loved ones to do the same. "Beating cervical cancer means beating it for everyone, and this move brings us closer to that goal." ENJOYED THIS STORY? analysis.brief_en: CIDRAP reported on August 27, 2026, that three new studies demonstrate that HPV vaccines significantly reduce the risk of infection in men, which can lead to cancers of the head and neck, anus, and penis. The findings highlight the broader benefits of HPV vaccination beyond its traditional role in preventing cervical cancer. These studies were published as part of CIDRAP's ongoing efforts to promote evidence-based vaccine information. The report does not specify the number of cases or deaths associated with HPV in men but emphasizes the protective effect of vaccination. The analysis is based on research findings and does not include any confirmed outbreak or public health emergency related to HPV in men. The studies suggest that HPV vaccines may offer substantial health benefits to males, contributing to the prevention of various HPV-associated diseases.

news.title_zh: 研究进一步证实HPV疫苗对男性有益 - CIDRAP
news.source_body_en: CIDRAP reported on August 27, 2026, that three new studies demonstrate that HPV vaccines significantly reduce the risk of infection in men, which can lead to cancers of the head and neck, anus, and penis. The findings highlight the broader benefits of HPV vaccination beyond its traditional role in preventing cervical cancer. These studies were published as part of CIDRAP's ongoing efforts to promote evidence-based vaccine information. The report does not specify the number of cases or deaths associated with HPV in men but emphasizes the protective effect of vaccination. The analysis is based on research findings and does not include any confirmed outbreak or public health emergency related to HPV in men. The studies suggest that HPV vaccines may offer substantial health benefits to males, contributing to the prevention of various HPV-associated diseases.
news.content_zh: CIDRAP于2026年8月27日报道,三项新研究表明,人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)疫苗显著降低男性感染风险,从而可预防头颈部癌症、肛门癌和阴茎癌。研究结果强调HPV疫苗在预防HPV相关疾病方面的广泛益处,超出其传统预防宫颈癌的作用。这些研究作为CIDRAP持续推广循证疫苗接种信息的一部分发表。报道未具体说明HPV在男性中的病例数或死亡数,但强调了HPV疫苗的保护效果。分析基于研究发现,未包含任何与HPV男性感染相关的确诊疫情或公共卫生紧急事件。研究表明HPV疫苗可能为男性提供显著健康益处,有助于预防多种HPV相关疾病。

cervical cancer – as at-home tests rolled out By Camilla Foster, PA 25/08/2026 The NHS has announced that women across England who have not attended their cervical screening appointments will be offered free at-home HPV testing kits. The rollout for these new self-testing kits began on Tuesday, August 25, in a bid to encourage more women to take part in screening for human papillomavirus (HPV), a virus that can increase the risk of cervical cancer. The kits include a vaginal swab, which allows women to collect a sample themselves at home. The sample can then be posted free of charge to an NHS laboratory, where it will be tested for high-risk HPV. If high-risk HPV is detected, the patient will be invited to attend a cervical screening appointment with a healthcare professional for further assessment. Following the announcement, we spoke to Dr Lucy Lord, founding partner and women’s health lead at Central Health London, who shared five important things every woman should know about cervical cancer... 1) HPV is very common, but only some types are high risk The human papillomavirus (HPV) causes almost all of the main types of cervical cancer (Alamy/PA) There are many different types of HPV and although most are harmless, some can cause changes that can develop into cancer. “HPV is a very common virus. If you are sexually active, you will have almost certainly caught at least one of the types of HPV viruses,” says Lord. Most people’s immune system clears about half of HPV infections within six to 12 months, but if you have a long-lasting (persistent) infection with a high-risk type of HPV you are more at risk of developing cervical cancer, according to Cancer Research UK’s website. Around 14 types of HPV are considered high risk for cervical cancer. Two of these types (HPV 16 and HPV 18) cause about 70 out of 100 (70%) of all cervical cancer cases, according to Cancer Research UK. “Some of them are oncogenic viruses, so are known to cause cancer,” says Lord. “They can insert themselves into the DNA of the vulnerable cells in the squamocolumnar junction [on the cervix], and cause mutations within those cells that turn them into cancer.” 2) The HPV vaccine offers effective protection against high-risk HPV strains and related cancers All children aged 12 to 13 (school year 8) are offered the HPV vaccine (Alamy/PA) The HPV vaccine helps protect against HPV and is recommended for children aged 12 to 13 years old and people at higher risk from HPV, according to the NHS website. “In private practice, we offer women in their 20s and 30s who missed being vaccinated a HPV vaccine,” says Lord. “Although it might not be cost-effective from a population perspective, it’s very effective for that individual, and it will still reduce the risk of them catching a virus that is around long enough to cause cancer.” 3) Irregular bleeding is a common symptom of cervical cancer “There are some indicators of cervical cancer. For example, irregular bleeding or bleeding in between your periods, and particularly bleeding after intercourse,” says Lord. “Abnormal discharge and blood stain discharge are also symptoms of cervical cancer.” Pain in your lower back, between your hip bones (pelvis), or in your lower tummy is also listed as another common symptom of cervical cancer on the NHS website. 4) Routine cervical screening can detect cellular changes before cancer forms Women are first invited for a cervical screening on the NHS from age 25 (Alamy/PA) “There are several stages (mild, moderate and severe) that can be detected before cancer develops,” says Lord. “A pap smear can spot abnormal or pre-malignant changes in the cells and there are several ways to treat the precancerous cells to stop them from becoming cancer.” All women aged 25 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, according to the NHS website. 5) Cervical cancer can be treated The treatment for cervical cancer depends on the size and type of cervical cancer you have, where the cancer is, if it has spread and on the patient’s general health. For some very early cervical cancers, it might be possible to remove all of the cancer with a large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or a cone biopsy, according to Cancer Research UK. “There are also different surgical procedures for cervical cancer, but if the cancer is too far advanced to be treated with a LLETZ biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are the standard treatments,” says Lord.
